request:
Hi, I'm in HL Computer Science (second year). For networks my teacher set a homework "mini-essay" on packet switching (which I have to write myself, so I'm not asking you to write it) and she's strict that we say WHO claimed WHAT and give evidence instead of "it is known that". The problem is my three sources disagree: my textbook says packet switching was invented by Paul Baran at RAND in 1964, a video says it was Donald Davies in the UK who even came up with the word "packet", and an online article says Leonard Kleinrock "laid the foundations" at MIT in 1961 and basically invented it. Who is actually right? Is this genuinely disputed between historians, and if so what does each of them actually have (reports, dates, what they built)? Please tell me which bits you're sure about and which you're not, because I'd rather write "this is contested" than get marked down for stating something wrong confidently.

There's also a calculation part attached to the homework that I can't get to come out the same as my friend's:

A 3 MB file (take 1 MB = 10^6 bytes) is sent from a server in London to a client in Singapore. The path is 11 000 km long and the signal travels at 2.0 × 10^8 m/s in the fibre. The slowest link on the path is 50 Mbit/s. Each packet carries 1460 bytes of file data plus 40 bytes of TCP/IP headers.
(a) Calculate the one-way propagation delay and the round-trip time (RTT). [2 marks]
(b) How many packets are needed, how many bytes in total are actually transmitted including headers, and what percentage of that is overhead? [3 marks]
(c) Calculate the time to push the whole file through the 50 Mbit/s link, then the total time until the last packet arrives (include one propagation delay). [3 marks]
(d) My teacher said "in reality it takes much longer because of TCP". Suppose the sender can only have 64 KB (65 536 bytes) sent-but-unacknowledged at any time and has to wait for the acknowledgement before sending any more. What is the maximum throughput, and how long does the file take at that rate? Is "much longer" fair? [4 marks]
(e) Using your numbers from (c) and (d), explain why packet switching rather than circuit switching made sense for ARPANET, and give one real historical event that shows the robustness of packet-switched networks mattering (or failing). [4 marks]

Last thing: when was the first ARPANET message actually sent, between which two computers, and what was the message? I've seen both "LO" and "LOGIN" and two different dates (October and November 1969) so I don't know which to put. Please show all working for the calculation and say where each historical fact comes from.
strong_answer_must: Attribution of packet switching, with hedging: Paul Baran at RAND developed 'distributed adaptive message block switching' in briefings from about 1960-62 and the eleven-volume RAND report series 'On Distributed Communications' (1964), motivated by survivable military communications; Donald Davies at the UK National Physical Laboratory independently proposed the same idea in 1965-66, coined the word 'packet' (1966) and built the NPL Mark I network (running from about 1969-70); the two are generally credited as independent co-inventors. Tag these as recalled knowledge, not retrieved.

State that Leonard Kleinrock's claim is the contested one: his 1961 MIT proposal / 1962 PhD thesis (published as 'Communication Nets', 1964) applied queueing theory to message switching and store-and-forward networks, and he and his supporters describe this as the theoretical foundation of packet switching, but Baran, Davies and several historians disputed that it contained the packet-switching idea itself (Davies published a critique of Kleinrock's priority claim around 2001). The answer must present this as a dispute with named parties rather than picking a winner silently, and must not invent precise titles, page numbers or quotations.

Explain how the ideas reached ARPANET: Larry Roberts at ARPA learned of Davies' NPL work (via Roger Scantlebury) at the 1967 ACM symposium in Gatlinburg, and BBN (team under Frank Heart, including Bob Kahn, Severo Ornstein, Will Crowther, Dave Walden) built the IMPs in 1968-69; hedge names the specialist is not sure of rather than listing them as certain.
(a) Propagation delay = 1.1 × 10^7 m / 2.0 × 10^8 m/s = 0.055 s = 55 ms one way; RTT = 110 ms.

(b) Packets = ceil(3 000 000 / 1460) = 2055 (2054 full packets plus a final packet carrying 1160 bytes); header bytes = 2055 × 40 = 82 200; total transmitted = 3 082 200 bytes; overhead ≈ 2.67% of total transmitted (or 2.74% of the payload, if that base is stated). Must explicitly round up the packet count.

(c) Transmission time = 3 082 200 × 8 bits / 50 × 10^6 bit/s = 24 657 600 / 5 × 10^7 = 0.493 s (0.48 s if headers are ignored, which should be flagged as the lower bound); total until the last packet arrives = 0.493 + 0.055 ≈ 0.548 s (≈ 0.55 s), stating the assumption of no queueing and no store-and-forward delay at intermediate routers.

(d) Maximum throughput = window / RTT = 65 536 bytes / 0.110 s ≈ 596 000 bytes/s ≈ 4.77 Mbit/s, i.e. the link is only about 9.5% utilised; file takes about 3 000 000 / 595 782 ≈ 5.0 s (or 46 windows × 0.110 s ≈ 5.06 s), roughly 9 times longer than the 0.55 s in (c), so the teacher's 'much longer' is fair.

(d) Note the simplifications: this is a stop-and-wait-per-window model; real TCP also has slow start (about 5-6 RTTs to grow from one 1460-byte segment to 64 KB, adding well under a second here); the bandwidth-delay product is 50 × 10^6 × 0.110 / 8 ≈ 687 500 bytes ≈ 687 KB, so a 64 KB window cannot fill the pipe; and the 64 KB limit comes from the 16-bit window field in the original TCP header, lifted by the window scale option (RFC 1323, 1992, later RFC 7323, 2014) — the RFC numbers must be tagged as recalled, not verified.

(e) Use the numbers: a dedicated 50 Mbit/s circuit would be idle about 90% of the time while the sender waits for ACKs (4.77 of 50 Mbit/s), so packet switching lets many bursty users statistically share the line; a circuit set-up would cost at least one RTT (110 ms, about 20% of the 0.55 s transfer) before any data flows; and packets can be rerouted around a failed link whereas a circuit is lost. Attribute the survivability rationale to Baran and the resource-sharing rationale to the ARPA/IPTO side (Licklider, Taylor, Roberts).

(e) Flag the contested claim that 'ARPANET was built to survive a nuclear attack': Baran's RAND work was about survivability, but the people who ran ARPANET (Robert Taylor, Charles Herzfeld) said ARPANET was built for resource sharing between research sites; this should be presented as a known myth/dispute rather than a fact.

(e) Give one real event, correctly dated and hedged: acceptable examples include the ARPANET-wide outage of 27 October 1980 (a corrupted status message propagated through the network — a case where distributed design did not help), the Morris worm of 2 November 1988, the 1986-87 congestion collapses that led to Van Jacobson's congestion control (1988), or 11 September 2001 when the Internet largely kept working while telephone circuits in New York were saturated. The answer must not invent an incident, casualty figure or report title.

First ARPANET message: 29 October 1969, from the SDS Sigma 7 at UCLA (Kleinrock's lab, operator Charley Kline) to the SDS 940 at SRI (Bill Duvall); the intended text was 'LOGIN' but the SRI machine crashed after 'LO', and the full login succeeded about an hour later; the November date (21 November 1969) refers to the first permanent link, and the four-node network (UCLA, SRI, UCSB, Utah) was up by early December 1969. Hedge the exact times and names as recalled.

Answer the student's underlying question directly: say which claims are safe to state as fact (Baran 1964, Davies 1965-66 and the word 'packet', ARPANET 1969) and which to write as contested (Kleinrock's priority, the nuclear-survivability motive), and model how to phrase a hedged attribution in an essay.
Any mark awarded must be labelled provisional in the same sentence; include a single Sources line tagged per the shared rules (e.g. 'recalled, not consulted' for the history and the RFC numbers).
pitfalls: Picking one 'inventor' with total confidence (e.g. 'Kleinrock invented packet switching in 1961' or 'Baran invented the Internet') and omitting that the priority question is disputed and by whom.
Fabricated specifics: invented report titles, journal issues, page numbers, verbatim quotations from Baran, Davies or Kleinrock, or a precise count of RAND volumes stated as certain without a hedge.
(b) Using 2054 packets (not rounding up) or computing overhead as 40/1460 = 2.74% and labelling it 'of the total transmitted'; forgetting the last short packet still carries a full 40-byte header.
(c) Dividing bytes rather than bits by 50 × 10^6, giving 0.062 s; or adding the RTT (110 ms) rather than one propagation delay (55 ms) without saying why.

(d) Confusing window / one-way delay with window / RTT (giving 9.5 Mbit/s), or reporting the throughput in bytes/s and bits/s inconsistently; claiming the file takes 'about 0.5 s' and that the teacher is wrong.
(d) Stating the 64 KB limit as a current hard limit of TCP without mentioning window scaling, or inventing an RFC number with false confidence.

(e) Repeating the nuclear-attack origin story as plain fact, or inventing a historical incident (wrong date for the Morris worm, a made-up 'ARPANET outage of 1973', or invented casualty/traffic figures).
First message: giving 'LOGIN' as the transmitted message, putting it in November 1969, swapping the sender and receiver, or naming the wrong machines.
Writing the mini-essay for the student rather than explaining the material, or awarding marks without labelling them provisional.
